The tutorial: one stage per idea, in the order the course teaches meter. Each stage has a lesson (HTML), the lines to practice it on (by citation), and optionally `practice`: the kinds of line its 'Practice more' link ticks -- `levels` (1 long and short only, 2 qu, 3 h/x/z, 4 elision, 5 muta cum liquida, 6 consonants at the start of a word, 7 Greek words, 8 advanced). Edit freely; the app checks that every citation exists. Content licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. A lesson may hold WORKED EXAMPLES:
shows a line from data/examples.json (lines from outside the reader) or from the reader, scanned, and divides the syllables data-show names -- a word, a colon, the vowel of its syllable, with #2 for a second one (colōremque:e#2) -- with the zoom-in's animation; a name that matches nothing is reported in the browser console. A stage may also carry `revised` (the date its lesson last grew, YYYY-MM-DD) and `new` (one line of HTML: what grew). A student who finished the stage BEFORE that date sees ✱ beside it and the `new` line atop its lesson, until they finish the stage again; set `revised` to the day AFTER the change is pushed -- the app records those dates in UTC, so an evening finish is already tomorrow, and a revision date on the push day itself would miss students who finished that morning. The cost of the day after is only that a student who finished on push day is shown the note once.

stages.title: Syllables, long and short
stages.new: a worked example from the first line of the Metamorphoses, divided before your eyes.
stages.lesson:
Scansion starts with syllables. Treat the whole line as one big word:

fistula disparibus paulātim surgit avēnīs
fistuladisparibuspaulātimsurgitavēnīs

Each vowel or diphthong gets a syllable. A diphthong is two vowels pronounced as one: ae, oe, au — sometimes ui, ei, eu. Split before one consonant, between two:

fis-tu-la-dis-pa-ri-bus-pau-lā-tim-sur-gi-ta-vē-nīs

Notice that avēnīs stole the final consonant of surgit!

A syllable is long if:

  • it has a long vowel (one marked with a macron: ā);
  • it has a diphthong;
  • it ends in a consonant — true whenever its vowel is followed by two or more consonants;
  • it is the last syllable of the line.

All other syllables are short.

All four at work in the first line of the Metamorphoses. Choose a syllable and watch it divided: the words run together into one big word, the consonants between two vowels drop into their syllables, and the reason for the mark lights up.

In this app you don't write the dashes. Drag a long mark ¯ or a short mark ˘ onto each vowel — the marks snap into place — and press Check.

stages.title: The pattern: dactyls and spondees
stages.lesson:
The hexameter is six feet, and each foot is one of two kinds:

  • a dactyl ¯ ˘ ˘ — Greek for “finger”: one long joint, then two short ones;
  • a spondee ¯ ¯ — equivalent to a dactyl, because two shorts make one long.

Every foot begins with a long syllable. The fifth foot is almost always a dactyl, and the sixth is always ¯ ¯.

When you press Check, dividers appear between the feet your marks make. If they stop partway through the line, that is where your marks stop fitting the pattern.

stages.title: Some refinements: qu, h, x, z, and letters that count twice
stages.new: worked examples, divided before your eyes, and the i that begins a word (iussit = jus-sit).
stages.lesson:
• qu: the u doesn't exist. It is neither a consonant nor a vowel, and has no effect on length.
  • h: also doesn't exist. It was very lightly pronounced.
  • x is actually two consonants, c + s — so dīxit et is dīc-si-tet.
  • z is also two consonants (it only shows up in Greek words).
  • i between two vowels is a consonant — say it like English y — and, like x, it counts as two: Troiae quī is Troj-jae-quī. The o has no macron, but its syllable ends in a consonant, so it is long.
  • hic and hoc before a vowel are really hicc and hocc: dabit hic in is da-bi-thic-cin. Short vowel, long syllable.
  • i at the start of a word, before a vowel, is a consonant too — iam, iussit, Iuppiter — but it counts only once: iussit et is jus-si-tet. So is an i after a prefix: coniugis is con-ju-gis.

stages.title: Elision
stages.new: worked examples from the Aeneid and Ovid's Golden Age, divided before your eyes.
stages.lesson:
Whenever a word ends in a vowel or m, and the next word begins with a vowel or h, one of the syllables gets eaten — elided. Delicious!

Generally it's the first one: atque ita = atqu' ita; Īcare, ait = Īcar' ait.

Unless the second word is est or es: imposita est = imposita 'st; ubi es = ubi 's.

Two elisions open Aeneas's story in Aeneid 2:

A final m goes with its vowel, and an h doesn't stop the elision. The Cyclops, in Aeneid 3:

And est after a vowel, in Ovid's Golden Age:

Mark an elision with the swoosh ‿ — drag it under the gap between the two syllables. The elided vowel turns grey and takes no long or short mark.

stages.title: Mūta cum liquida
stages.new: one word scanned both ways in a single line of Ovid, divided before your eyes.
stages.lesson:
Mutes are hard sounds that fully interrupt the flow of air: c, g; t, d; p, b. Liquids are just two: l, r.

(s and f are fricatives, i/j and v are semivowels, and m and n are nasals: none of them matter here.)

In actual speech, a mute + liquid usually began a syllable: patris was pa-tris, with the first syllable short. In poetry, either pronunciation was permitted — pat-ris, first syllable long, or pa-tris, first syllable short. Let the rest of the line decide.

Ovid scans the same word both ways in a single line. The ashes of Memnon's pyre take shape as a bird, at first like a bird, soon a true bird:

stages.title: Consonants at the start of a word
stages.new: two worked examples, divided before your eyes.
stages.lesson:
In Greek, two consonants at the start of a word tend to lengthen the last vowel of the word before. Not so much in Latin:

atque ita compositās parvō curvāmine flectit

The -e of curvāmine stays short before fl-. A short vowel before a mute + liquid that begins the next word usually stays short too: unda gravet.

Two more from the opening of the Metamorphoses: a mute + liquid that begins a word, and fl-.

stages.title: Greek words
stages.new: two worked examples, āēr and Eurydicē, divided before your eyes.
stages.lesson:
Most of the names in these stories are Greek, and Greek words put vowels together in ways Latin usually doesn't. Trust the macrons, and watch for:

  • pairs that look like diphthongs but aren't: āera is ā-e-ra, three syllables; Pāsiphaē ends -pha-ē;
  • vowels side by side: Mīnōia, Boōtēn, Aenēās;
  • the diphthong eu in names like Teucrī.

Ovid's āēr is two syllables, ā-ēr: the macrons say so.

And Orpheus, begging the gods below to give Eurydice back, begins his line with the diphthong eu:

stages.title: The poets' licences
stages.new: a worked example of each licence, divided before your eyes.
stages.lesson:
Now and then a poet bends the rules. You won't meet these often, but you'll learn to recognize them:

  • Hiatus: no elision where you'd expect one — dea. ille. An interjection like Ō never elides — Narcissus, in love with his own reflection:
  • Synizesis: two vowels in one word run together into a single syllable — Lāvīnia becomes Lā-vīn-ja. Mark it with the swoosh between the two vowels. Dido's hall has lamps hanging from golden ceilings, aureīs:
  • Hypermetry: the line has one syllable too many, and its last vowel elides into the next line — locōrumque. Put the swoosh after the last syllable. Mercury, appearing to Aeneas in a dream; the next line begins et:
